title: Golden Testcases You Can Check With a Calculator
gist: Ramtera's founder argues that static timing engines should be validated first on tiny golden testcases where every reported digit can be re-derived by hand, because correlation against a reference tool proves only agreement, not correctness. He applies this to cell and wire delays, SDC exception priority, SPEF parsing and multi-host multi-corner runs.

insights.claim: Validating a new timing engine by correlating slack against an established tool only proves agreement; it inherits the reference's approximations and bugs, cannot say which tool is right when they disagree, and cannot catch errors both share.
insights.speaker: Sameer Pawanekar
insights.so_what: Correlation-only sign-off for EDA tools hides shared errors, a quality risk for new entrants and incumbents.
insights.quote: Correlation is useful, but it only proves agreement.
insights.locator: The problem: agreement is not correctness

insights.claim: Ramtera's rule is that correctness is proven first on testcases small enough to re-derive every number with a calculator, with large-design correlation afterward testing modelling, never arithmetic; a digit that cannot be re-derived is a bug by definition.
insights.speaker: Sameer Pawanekar
insights.so_what: Defines a verification discipline that separates arithmetic errors from modelling differences.
insights.locator: The problem: agreement is not correctness

insights.claim: Once arithmetic is proven on golden testcases, any remaining large-design disagreement must come from modelling choices, which makes correlation meaningful.
insights.speaker: Sameer Pawanekar
insights.so_what: Golden cases make correlation results interpretable rather than replacing them.
insights.quote: Golden testcases don’t replace large-design correlation.
insights.locator: A checklist you can use on any timing engine

themes.theme: Golden testcase design and worked arithmetic

insights.claim: The golden testcase uses a two-cell library with single-row delay tables, a four-instance netlist with one register, and simple parasitics, and requires re-deriving cell arc delays by interpolation, wire delays by the Elmore formula, and required times.
insights.speaker: Sameer Pawanekar
insights.so_what: Concrete recipe for a hand-checkable timing benchmark.
insights.locator: The approach: a design you can hold in your head

insights.claim: The engine passes only if it reproduces every printed digit; 'close' is a failure.
insights.speaker: Sameer Pawanekar
insights.so_what: Sets an exact-match acceptance bar for timing tools.

insights.claim: In the worked example, a register delay of 0.0675 ns derives from a table running 0.065 ns at 0.01 pF to 0.090 ns at 0.05 pF at a 0.014 pF load, and a wire delay of 5.5 ps equals 250 ohm x 0.014 pF plus 250 ohm x 0.008 pF.
insights.speaker: Sameer Pawanekar
insights.so_what: Shows the checks are feasible by hand and reproducible by the engine.
insights.locator: Results: one path, every digit accounted for

insights.claim: In the worked example every report line matches its hand derivation, including hold checks, across setup and hold and four constraint mechanisms, so a mismatch would point directly at the lookup, wire or required-time term.
insights.speaker: Sameer Pawanekar
insights.so_what: Golden cases provide fault localization, not just pass/fail.

insights.claim: Timing tools disagree most quietly on path exceptions, where SDC priority has false path over max/min delay over multicycle, then more-specific selectors, with -from outranking -to and -to outranking -through.
insights.speaker: Sameer Pawanekar
insights.so_what: Exception handling is a common hidden source of cross-tool timing differences.
insights.quote: Timing tools disagree most quietly on path exceptions
insights.locator: Exceptions: test the semantics against documented examples

insights.claim: Ramtera's implementation reproduces 8 of 8 documented SDC exception example pairs, and arithmetic checks include a 0.30 ns max-delay giving a required time of 0.2000 ns and a setup multicycle of 3 moving the hold required time to 1.6300 ns.
insights.speaker: Sameer Pawanekar
insights.so_what: Vendor-reported conformance results against documented examples.

insights.claim: A SPEF reader has room for subtle errors in unit multipliers, name maps, dividers, corner triplets and multi-file stitching, so a SPEF small enough to evaluate on paper should be required to match; the reference tree gives Elmore delays of 3.000 ps and 3.500 ps and a driver load of 0.020 pF.
insights.speaker: Sameer Pawanekar
insights.so_what: Parasitic ingestion errors silently corrupt post-route timing.

insights.claim: Accepting a distributed multi-corner run on a design where every view has zero slack is a mistake, because a corner's RC scaling lost in transit would still match.
insights.speaker: Sameer Pawanekar
insights.so_what: Acceptance tests must use cases that cannot pass by accident.
insights.quote: A common mistake is accepting a distributed run on a design where every view has zero slack.
insights.locator: Multi-corner, multi-host: accept only exact equality

insights.claim: Using RC corners scaled by 1.4x and 0.8x under a 0.14 ns clock, a two-host run matched the local run for every view, with worst-RC setup WNS/TNS of -0.0948 ns and best-RC setup of -0.0841 ns.
insights.speaker: Sameer Pawanekar
insights.so_what: Vendor evidence that distributed MMMC analysis is exact, relevant to runtime scaling.
